items.stem: Which method is most closely associated with social and cultural anthropology?
items.answer: Long-term participant observation
items.markingKey: Long-term participant observation. Long-term participant observation (fieldwork) is the defining method of SCA.

items.stem: "Anthropologists only study small, remote, 'traditional' societies." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Anthropologists study every kind of society, including cities, corporations, hospitals and online worlds; Bourgois studied crack dealers in New York and Boellstorff studied Second Life.
items.markingKey: Anthropologists study every kind of society, including cities, corporations, hospitals and online worlds; Bourgois studied crack dealers in New York and Boellstorff studied Second Life. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between social and cultural anthropology and sociology.
items.answer: Both study social life, but anthropology traditionally relies on long-term participant observation and holistic, comparative study of small-scale or local settings, whereas sociology more often uses surveys and statistics to study large-scale patterns in industrial societies; the boundary is now blurred.
items.markingKey: Both study social life, but anthropology traditionally relies on long-term participant observation and holistic, comparative study of small-scale or local settings, whereas sociology more often uses surveys and statistics to study large-scale patterns in industrial societies; the boundary is now blurred. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the bus depot on the edge of the city, Wairimu sells boiled eggs and peeled oranges from a tray balanced on a crate. "I am not a hawker," she tells me firmly. "Hawkers run. I have my place." Her place is a square of pavement she rents informally from the man who sweeps the depot each morning. When conductors shout the names of destinations, she calls back their nicknames. On Sundays she brings eggs to the sweeper's family instead of money. Twice a month the county askaris clear the pavement, and on those days Wairimu sits on the bus with her tray, "travelling" until they leave.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a bus depot in a Kenyan town.

Using the key concept of identity, explain why Wairimu insists that she is "not a hawker". Link the actions described to wider social, economic or political conditions.
items.answer: Her claim is an emic category that asserts status and identity: having "a place" signals legitimacy, belonging and respectability compared with mobile hawkers. Her security rests on social relations (sweeper, conductors) rather than legal title, so identity and place are produced through relationships and contested by state power (askaris).
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Her claim is an emic category that asserts status and identity: having "a place" signals legitimacy, belonging and respectability compared with mobile hawkers. Her security rests on social relations (sweeper, conductors) rather than legal title, so identity and place are produced through relationships and contested by state power (askaris). Markbands – 4: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 2–3: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Horace Miner's "Body Ritual among the Nacirema" (1956) shows the familiar made strange.
items.answer: Miner described Americans' bathroom routines, dentists and doctors as strange magical rites of the "Nacirema". It shows that an outsider's (etic) description can make one's own culture look exotic, revealing ethnocentric assumptions in how "others" are described.
items.markingKey: Context (Miner described Americans' bathroom routines, dentists and doctors as strange magical rites of the "Nacirema".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it shows that an outsider's (etic) description can make one's own culture look exotic, revealing ethnocentric assumptions in how "others" are described. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the familiar made strange.

Compare and contrast how identity is experienced by the people in the text and by the people in one other ethnography you have studied (for example Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995)). Your answer should identify both similarities and differences.
items.answer: Text: Her claim is an emic category that asserts status and identity: having "a place" signals legitimacy, belonging and respectability compared with mobile hawkers. Her security rests on social relations (sweeper, conductors) rather than legal title, so identity and place are produced through relationships and contested by state power (askaris). Ethnography – Philippe Bourgois, In Search of Respect: Selling Crack in El Barrio (1995), among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990): Dealers built a "street culture" of resistance in which they sought the respect and dignity denied to them in mainstream work, yet that culture also drew them into self-destruction and violence. Comparison: similarities and differences in how identity is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An insider's view: the categories, meanings and explanations used by members of the group being studied"?
options: belonging
space-place-time
power
emic perspective
items.answer: emic perspective
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of emic perspective.

items.stem: Briefly explain why holism is important for understanding a single practice such as bridewealth.
items.answer: Bridewealth only makes sense in relation to kinship (which group gains rights to children), economy (cattle or money), politics (alliances) and values (respect); studying it in isolation could mislead an observer into seeing it as "buying a wife".
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Bridewealth only makes sense in relation to kinship (which group gains rights to children), economy (cattle or money), politics (alliances) and values (respect); studying it in isolation could mislead an observer into seeing it as "buying a wife". (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Read the text below.

— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a bus depot in a Kenyan town.

Identify and describe the ways in which Wairimu secures her place to trade. Refer closely to the text. You do not need to refer to any other ethnography in this answer.
items.answer: She rents a square of pavement informally from the sweeper; she pays partly in eggs (gifts) to his family rather than money; she maintains friendly relations with conductors through nicknames; she avoids the county officers by sitting on a bus during clearances; she distinguishes herself from "hawkers" who run.

Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: Outline how culture shapes the holistic and comparative study of human societies, using evidence from Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific.
items.answer: Malinowski argued that institutions such as the kula and garden magic meet social and psychological needs, and insisted on grasping "the native's point of view" through long-term participant observation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Malinowski argued that institutions such as the kula and garden magic meet social and psychological needs, and insisted on grasping "the native's point of view" through long-term participant observation. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Bronisław Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to culture. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: "The emic perspective should always take priority over the etic perspective." Discuss with reference to at least one ethnography you have studied.
items.answer: Neither should always dominate: good ethnography moves between emic and etic perspectives.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: it respects people's own understandings and avoids imposing outside categories; it counters the colonial history of describing others in the observer's terms; insiders may not see wider structures such as global markets or state power; people within a group disagree, so there is rarely a single emic view; etic concepts enable comparison and critique. Suitable ethnographies include Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific, Miner's "Body Ritual among the Nacirema", Boas's historical particularism. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Neither should always dominate: good ethnography moves between emic and etic perspectives. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "materiality"?
options: An outsider's or analyst's view: categories and explanations developed by the observer to describe and compare across societies
The ways people come to feel and be recognised as members of groups, places or communities, and the processes of inclusion and exclusion that this involves
The significance of physical objects, bodies and environments in social life, including how things shape and express relationships, identities and meanings
Judging other cultures by the standards and values of one's own, usually assuming one's own ways are natural or superior
items.answer: The significance of physical objects, bodies and environments in social life, including how things shape and express relationships, identities and meanings
items.markingKey: C. "materiality" is the significance of physical objects, bodies and environments in social life, including how things shape and express relationships, identities and meanings.

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Materiality simply means how much money or property people have." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Materiality concerns the social meanings and effects of objects, bodies and environments, not only wealth; a kula armshell or a banana-leaf bundle may have little monetary value but great social significance.
items.markingKey: Materiality concerns the social meanings and effects of objects, bodies and environments, not only wealth; a kula armshell or a banana-leaf bundle may have little monetary value but great social significance. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between belonging and identity.
items.answer: Identity is how individuals and groups define who they are (and are defined by others); belonging is the experience and recognition of membership in a group or place, including who is included or excluded.
items.markingKey: Identity is how individuals and groups define who they are (and are defined by others); belonging is the experience and recognition of membership in a group or place, including who is included or excluded. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to Geertz's study of the Balinese cockfight, explain how it illustrates how one practice illustrates several key concepts.
items.answer: Men wagered on cocks according to kin and village ties, and deep matches between high-status men put status symbolically at stake. The cockfight shows power (status hierarchy), identity (masculinity), social relations (betting alliances) and culture (a text Balinese tell about themselves).
items.markingKey: Context (Men wagered on cocks according to kin and village ties, and deep matches between high-status men put status symbolically at stake.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the cockfight shows power (status hierarchy), identity (masculinity), social relations (betting alliances) and culture (a text Balinese tell about themselves). – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how one practice illustrates several key concepts.

items.stem: Using Geertz's "Deep Play" (in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958)) as your example, describe how power is shown.
items.answer: In "deep" matches between high-status men the money matters less than the status symbolically at stake, so the cockfight dramatises the village status hierarchy without actually changing it.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: In "deep" matches between high-status men the money matters less than the status symbolically at stake, so the cockfight dramatises the village status hierarchy without actually changing it. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Clifford Geertz, "Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight" (1972; reprinted in The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973), in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the Saturday clothing market of Kotei, sellers unpack bales of second-hand garments shipped from Europe. Buyers call the clothes "dead white men's clothes", though the sellers prefer "obroni wawu". Ama, who has sold there for twenty years, opens each bale like a lottery. "One bale feeds my children for a month, another one is rags." Her stall is her late mother's, and older traders still greet her by her mother's name. When a city council project proposed moving the market to a new concrete building, the traders marched with their best garments draped across their shoulders.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a second-hand clothing market in Ghana.

With reference to the concept of materiality, analyse how the second-hand clothes connect the market traders to wider relations of power. Support each step of your explanation with evidence from the extract.
items.answer: The bales link traders to global flows of discarded Western goods, over which they have no control; the names given to the clothes comment on that inequality; the council's relocation plan shows state power over space; the traders turn the clothes into a symbol in protest, showing materiality as a resource for resisting power.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The bales link traders to global flows of discarded Western goods, over which they have no control; the names given to the clothes comment on that inequality; the council's relocation plan shows state power over space; the traders turn the clothes into a symbol in protest, showing materiality as a resource for resisting power. Markbands – 5–6: clear, well-supported explanation that analyses the text using relevant anthropological concepts and terminology; 3–4: some explanation with relevant points from the text; a key concept is used, though analysis is uneven; 1–2: limited understanding; mostly description or paraphrase of the text, concepts absent or misused; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Power is the most important key concept in social and cultural anthropology."
items.answer: Power is pervasive and frequently central, but its importance depends on the question and it is best analysed together with other concepts.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: power shapes classification, belonging and identity; ethnographies such as Bourgois and Holmes show structural power explaining suffering. Arguments against: an exclusive focus on power can neglect meaning, emotion and creativity; concepts such as materiality and space-place-time reveal dimensions of life not reducible to power; the concepts are interdependent. Supported judgement: Power is pervasive and frequently central, but its importance depends on the question and it is best analysed together with other concepts.

items.stem: Big question: "Can an anthropologist ever fully understand another way of life?" Discuss with reference to the key concept of belonging and at least one ethnography you have studied, such as Basso's Wisdom Sits in Places.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies belonging explicitly and uses ethnography: Knowing the names and stories of the land is part of belonging to the community and links people across generations. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies belonging explicitly and uses ethnography: Knowing the names and stories of the land is part of belonging to the community and links people across generations. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion. Markbands – 9–10: perceptive, well-argued response integrating key concepts, ethnography and theory, with a reasoned conclusion; 7–8: clear argument that applies the key concept to ethnographic material and considers more than one perspective; 5–6: relevant response using a key concept and an ethnography, with some analysis; 3–4: some relevant ideas; ethnographic or conceptual support is thin or general; 1–2: limited response to the big question; assertions with little anthropological support; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Explain why materiality matters to anthropologists who study meaning.
items.answer: Meanings are carried and made by things – clothing, houses, gifts, bodies – so analysing objects shows how values and relationships become tangible and durable.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Meanings are carried and made by things – clothing, houses, gifts, bodies – so analysing objects shows how values and relationships become tangible and durable. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the key concepts overlap with one another.
items.answer: Social life is integrated: belonging involves power over who is included, identity is often expressed through materiality, and classification shapes social relations, so one ethnographic example usually illustrates several concepts.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Social life is integrated: belonging involves power over who is included, identity is often expressed through materiality, and classification shapes social relations, so one ethnographic example usually illustrates several concepts. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Evaluate the ethical challenges of researching, writing and publishing an account such as the one in the text. Refer to specific situations in the text rather than listing general principles.
items.answer: The researcher must obtain consent from traders who may fear the council, avoid identifying individuals involved in protests, and consider how publishing names (e.g. Ama, her mother's name) might expose them; findings should be shared with the traders' association. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Judging other cultures by the standards and values of one's own, usually assuming one's own ways are natural or superior"?
options: moral relativism
comparison
ethnocentrism
universalism
items.answer: ethnocentrism
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of ethnocentrism.

items.stem: Explain the difference between ethnocentrism and cultural relativism.
items.answer: Ethnocentrism judges others by one's own standards and assumes their superiority; cultural relativism seeks to understand practices in terms of their own cultural logic before judging.
items.markingKey: Ethnocentrism judges others by one's own standards and assumes their superiority; cultural relativism seeks to understand practices in terms of their own cultural logic before judging. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Leila writes: "Only Westerners are ethnocentric." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Ethnocentrism is a general human tendency found in all societies; anthropology tries to counter it everywhere, including in the anthropologist's own assumptions.
items.markingKey: Ethnocentrism is a general human tendency found in all societies; anthropology tries to counter it everywhere, including in the anthropologist's own assumptions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping (among shantytown women of the Alto do Cruzeiro, Bom Jesus da Mata, north-east Brazil (fieldwork 1960s–1980s)) as your example, describe how culture is shown.
items.answer: She argues that mother love is not a universal instinct but is shaped by economic and demographic conditions, challenging Western assumptions about motherhood.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: She argues that mother love is not a universal instinct but is shaped by economic and demographic conditions, challenging Western assumptions about motherhood. Award up to [3]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Nancy Scheper-Hughes, Death without Weeping: The Violence of Everyday Life in Brazil (1992), among shantytown women of the Alto do Cruzeiro, Bom Jesus da Mata, north-east Brazil (fieldwork 1960s–1980s)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to culture. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The volunteer group arrived in the village with a truck of solar cookers. At the meeting, their leader explained that cooking over wood fires was "unhealthy and backward". The women listened politely. Three months later most cookers stood in a storeroom. Kadi explained to me that the evening fire is where daughters learn recipes and where neighbours stop to talk, and that the solar cooker "works only when the sun is at its highest, when we are in the fields". She uses hers to dry chillies. "They wanted us to be modern," she laughed, "but they never asked when we cook."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a rural village in the Sahel region of West Africa.

Describe how the women in the text responded to the solar cookers, as presented in the text. Refer to at least three specific details from the text.
items.answer: They listened politely at the meeting; most cookers were left in a storeroom; Kadi explained why the evening fire matters (learning recipes, talking with neighbours); she pointed out the timing problem (sun at midday while women are in the fields); she repurposed the cooker to dry chillies.
items.markingKey: They listened politely at the meeting; most cookers were left in a storeroom; Kadi explained why the evening fire matters (learning recipes, talking with neighbours); she pointed out the timing problem (sun at midday while women are in the fields); she repurposed the cooker to dry chillies. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that cultural relativism prevents anthropologists from criticising harmful practices? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Methodological relativism does not prevent criticism; it makes criticism better informed and more respectful of local voices.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: strict relativism could imply no basis for criticism; relativist arguments have sometimes been used to defend abuses as "tradition"; relativism is primarily a method of understanding, not a moral endpoint; Scheper-Hughes and Abu-Lughod show anthropologists combining contextual understanding with ethical judgement; insiders themselves often contest harmful practices, so there is no single "cultural" view. Suitable ethnographies include Miner's "Body Ritual among the Nacirema", Boas's historical particularism, Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Methodological relativism does not prevent criticism; it makes criticism better informed and more respectful of local voices. items.answer: Judging other cultures by the standards and values of one's own, usually assuming one's own ways are natural or superior

items.stem: Explain why othering can have political consequences.
items.answer: Representing groups as backward or dangerous can justify intervention, discrimination or exclusion – for example colonial rule or the "saving Muslim women" rhetoric criticised by Abu-Lughod.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Representing groups as backward or dangerous can justify intervention, discrimination or exclusion – for example colonial rule or the "saving Muslim women" rhetoric criticised by Abu-Lughod. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The volunteer group arrived in the village with a truck of solar cookers. At the meeting, their leader explained that cooking over wood fires was "unhealthy and backward". The women listened politely. Three months later most cookers stood in a storeroom. Kadi explained to me that the evening fire is where daughters learn recipes and where neighbours stop to talk, and that the solar cooker "works only when the sun is at its highest, when we are in the fields". She uses hers to dry chillies. "They wanted us to be modern," she laughed, "but they never asked when we cook."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a rural village in the Sahel region of West Africa.

With reference to the concept of culture, analyse why the volunteers' project can be described as ethnocentric. Support each step of your explanation with evidence from the extract.
items.answer: The volunteers judged wood fires as "backward" by their own standards and assumed their technology was superior; they did not study when, how and why women cook (an emic perspective); the fire's social meaning (teaching daughters, sociability) and the women's work schedule were ignored, so the project failed, while women reinterpreted the object in their own terms.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The volunteers judged wood fires as "backward" by their own standards and assumed their technology was superior; they did not study when, how and why women cook (an emic perspective); the fire's social meaning (teaching daughters, sociability) and the women's work schedule were ignored, so the project failed, while women reinterpreted the object in their own terms. items.stem: Briefly describe Abu-Lughod's critique of the "saving Muslim women" discourse after 2001 and explain what it reveals about othering and the limits of ethnocentric judgement.
items.answer: She showed how images of veiled Afghan women were used to justify the war in Afghanistan, while ignoring women's own priorities and the harms of intervention. It shows that portraying women as passive victims of "their culture" erases their agency and serves political ends; she argues for respecting different ideas of a good life while still opposing injustice.
items.markingKey: Context (She showed how images of veiled Afghan women were used to justify the war in Afghanistan, while ignoring women's own priorities and the harms of intervention.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: it shows that portraying women as passive victims of "their culture" erases their agency and serves political ends; she argues for respecting different ideas of a good life while still opposing injustice. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to othering and the limits of ethnocentric judgement.

items.stem: Which of the following is one of the key concepts of IB Social and Cultural Anthropology?
options: Sovereignty
Natural selection
Materiality
Supply and demand
items.answer: Materiality
items.markingKey: C. Materiality is one of the course key concepts; the others belong to politics, economics and biology.

items.stem: Define the term "emic perspective".
items.answer: An insider's view: the categories, meanings and explanations used by members of the group being studied
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an insider's view: the categories, meanings and explanations used by members of the group being studied. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: What was the main purpose of Horace Miner's "Body Ritual among the Nacirema" (1956)?
items.answer: To show how ethnographic description can make familiar practices seem exotic
items.markingKey: To show how ethnographic description can make familiar practices seem exotic. The "Nacirema" are Americans; the satire exposes ethnocentric description.

items.stem: Distinguish between identity and belonging.
items.answer: Identity is how individuals and groups define who they are (and are defined by others); belonging is the experience and recognition of membership in a group or place, including who is included or excluded.
items.markingKey: Identity is how individuals and groups define who they are (and are defined by others); belonging is the experience and recognition of membership in a group or place, including who is included or excluded. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why anthropology is said to make "the strange familiar and the familiar strange".
items.answer: By explaining unfamiliar practices in their context, anthropology makes them intelligible (strange made familiar); by applying the same analysis to our own customs, as Miner did with the "Nacirema", it exposes taken-for-granted assumptions (familiar made strange).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: By explaining unfamiliar practices in their context, anthropology makes them intelligible (strange made familiar); by applying the same analysis to our own customs, as Miner did with the "Nacirema", it exposes taken-for-granted assumptions (familiar made strange). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Cultural relativism means anthropologists must accept every practice as morally good." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Cultural relativism is a method for understanding; anthropologists such as Scheper-Hughes argue for ethical engagement after understanding (the "primacy of the ethical").
items.markingKey: Cultural relativism is a method for understanding; anthropologists such as Scheper-Hughes argue for ethical engagement after understanding (the "primacy of the ethical"). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the key concepts are useful when reading an unfamiliar ethnography.
items.answer: They provide a common analytical vocabulary that directs attention to recurring dimensions of social life (power, identity, materiality, etc.), so a reader can analyse new material systematically and compare it with other ethnographies.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They provide a common analytical vocabulary that directs attention to recurring dimensions of social life (power, identity, materiality, etc.), so a reader can analyse new material systematically and compare it with other ethnographies. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between an etic perspective and an emic perspective.
items.answer: An emic perspective uses the meanings and categories of the people studied; an etic perspective uses the analyst's categories, which allow cross-cultural comparison but may not be recognised by participants.
items.markingKey: An emic perspective uses the meanings and categories of the people studied; an etic perspective uses the analyst's categories, which allow cross-cultural comparison but may not be recognised by participants. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between cultural relativism and ethnocentrism.
items.answer: Ethnocentrism judges others by one's own standards and assumes their superiority; cultural relativism seeks to understand practices in terms of their own cultural logic before judging.
items.markingKey: Ethnocentrism judges others by one's own standards and assumes their superiority; cultural relativism seeks to understand practices in terms of their own cultural logic before judging. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the Saturday clothing market of Kotei, sellers unpack bales of second-hand garments shipped from Europe. Buyers call the clothes "dead white men's clothes", though the sellers prefer "obroni wawu". Ama, who has sold there for twenty years, opens each bale like a lottery. "One bale feeds my children for a month, another one is rags." Her stall is her late mother's, and older traders still greet her by her mother's name. When a city council project proposed moving the market to a new concrete building, the traders marched with their best garments draped across their shoulders.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a second-hand clothing market in Ghana.

Identify and describe how the traders in the text depend on and use clothing. Refer closely to the text. You do not need to refer to any other ethnography in this answer.
items.answer: Bales are opened unseen and their contents determine income ("feeds my children" or "rags"); clothing has names that carry meaning ("obroni wawu"); stalls are inherited (Ama's mother's stall); traders wore their best garments during the protest march.
items.markingKey: Bales are opened unseen and their contents determine income ("feeds my children" or "rags"); clothing has names that carry meaning ("obroni wawu"); stalls are inherited (Ama's mother's stall); traders wore their best garments during the protest march. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: With reference to one anthropological text you have studied, for example Boas's historical particularism, explain the relevance of culture to the holistic and comparative study of human societies.
items.answer: Boas argued that each culture is the product of its own history and must be understood in its own terms (historical particularism), rejecting rankings of cultures as "savage" or "civilised".
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Boas argued that each culture is the product of its own history and must be understood in its own terms (historical particularism), rejecting rankings of cultures as "savage" or "civilised". Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: With reference to Basso's work with the Western Apache of Cibecue, explain how it illustrates space-place-time.
items.answer: Apache speakers used place-names and their stories to remind wrongdoers of ancestral lessons. It shows that space becomes place through names, stories and memory, and that places carry moral and historical meaning.

items.stem: A student claims: "An etic account is always more objective and therefore better than an emic one." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Etic categories are also cultural products of the analyst's background; emic and etic accounts answer different questions and are strongest when combined.
items.markingKey: Etic categories are also cultural products of the analyst's background; emic and etic accounts answer different questions and are strongest when combined. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Scheper-Hughes's "The Primacy of the Ethical" (1995) shows the limits of cultural relativism.
items.answer: Scheper-Hughes argued that anthropologists cannot hide behind relativism when faced with suffering such as the infant deaths she witnessed in north-east Brazil. She calls for a "militant" anthropology that understands context but also takes moral responsibility, showing that relativism as method need not mean moral neutrality.

Explain how the second-hand clothes connect the market traders to wider relations of power, using one or more anthropological concepts. Link the actions described to wider social, economic or political conditions.
items.answer: The bales link traders to global flows of discarded Western goods, over which they have no control; the names given to the clothes comment on that inequality; the council's relocation plan shows state power over space; the traders turn the clothes into a symbol in protest, showing materiality as a resource for resisting power.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the bus depot on the edge of the city, Wairimu sells boiled eggs and peeled oranges from a tray balanced on a crate. "I am not a hawker," she tells me firmly. "Hawkers run. I have my place." Her place is a square of pavement she rents informally from the man who sweeps the depot each morning. When conductors shout the names of destinations, she calls back their nicknames. On Sundays she brings eggs to the sweeper's family instead of money. Twice a month the county askaris clear the pavement, and on those days Wairimu sits on the bus with her tray, "travelling" until they leave.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a bus depot in a Kenyan town.

Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. Refer to specific situations in the text rather than listing general principles.
items.answer: Traders in informal economies may be vulnerable to state officers, so anonymity, pseudonyms and care with details of the informal rental and avoidance tactics are essential; consent must be informed and ongoing; the researcher must avoid drawing official attention to the depot. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: "Power is central to understanding the way people judge other ways of life." Compare and contrast two anthropological studies, for example Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments and Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping, in the light of this claim.
items.answer: Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments (among the Awlad 'Ali Bedouin of Egypt's Western Desert (fieldwork from 1978)): Women and young men – those with less power – express love, loss and vulnerability through short ghinnawa poems, a socially acceptable channel for sentiments that would breach the honour code if spoken directly. Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping (among shantytown women of the Alto do Cruzeiro, Bom Jesus da Mata, north-east Brazil (fieldwork 1960s–1980s)): She describes the "everyday violence" of poverty, in which hunger is medicalised as nervos and treated with tranquillisers and vitamins, hiding the political causes of suffering. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Bourgois's In Search of Respect and Geertz's "Deep Play", compare and contrast the role of identity in the analysis of everyday social life.
items.answer: Bourgois's In Search of Respect (among Puerto Rican crack dealers in East Harlem, New York (fieldwork 1985–1990)): Dealers built a "street culture" of resistance in which they sought the respect and dignity denied to them in mainstream work, yet that culture also drew them into self-destruction and violence. Geertz's "Deep Play" (in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958)): Men identify closely with their cocks, and the Balinese word for cock is used metaphorically for heroes, champions and ladies' men, so the fights express masculine identity and rivalry. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far identity is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: "Is there such a thing as a universal human experience?" With reference to Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa and the key concept of culture, evaluate possible answers to this question.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies culture explicitly and uses ethnography: Mead argued that adolescence in Samoa was relatively free of the stress seen in the United States, supporting Boas's view that culture rather than biology shapes development; Derek Freeman's 1983 critique disputed her findings. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

items.stem: Define the term "power".
items.answer: The capacity to influence or control people, resources and meanings, exercised through force, institutions, knowledge and everyday practice
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the capacity to influence or control people, resources and meanings, exercised through force, institutions, knowledge and everyday practice. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "comparison"?
options: The patterned ties – of kinship, friendship, exchange, hierarchy or conflict – that connect people to one another
An outsider's or analyst's view: categories and explanations developed by the observer to describe and compare across societies
Representing a group as fundamentally different from and inferior to "us", often by stressing exotic or unchanging traits
The anthropological method of placing practices from different societies side by side to identify similarities, differences and broader patterns
items.answer: The anthropological method of placing practices from different societies side by side to identify similarities, differences and broader patterns
items.markingKey: D. "comparison" is the anthropological method of placing practices from different societies side by side to identify similarities, differences and broader patterns.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "ethnocentrism"?
options: The capacity to influence or control people, resources and meanings, exercised through force, institutions, knowledge and everyday practice
The comparative study of human societies and cultures, based mainly on long-term fieldwork, that seeks to understand how people make sense of and organise their social lives
Judging other cultures by the standards and values of one's own, usually assuming one's own ways are natural or superior
The ways people come to feel and be recognised as members of groups, places or communities, and the processes of inclusion and exclusion that this involves
items.answer: Judging other cultures by the standards and values of one's own, usually assuming one's own ways are natural or superior
items.markingKey: C. "ethnocentrism" is judging other cultures by the standards and values of one's own, usually assuming one's own ways are natural or superior.

items.stem: "Power is only visible when someone uses violence." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Power is often hidden in everyday routines, norms and categories – for example in the status contests of Geertz's cockfight or in the symbolic violence described by Holmes.
items.markingKey: Power is often hidden in everyday routines, norms and categories – for example in the status contests of Geertz's cockfight or in the symbolic violence described by Holmes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why anthropologists value both emic and etic perspectives.
items.answer: Emic accounts show how people themselves understand their practices, avoiding distortion by outside categories; etic analysis allows comparison and can reveal patterns or structures (e.g. power, economy) of which participants are unaware. Combining them gives a fuller, more rigorous account.

items.stem: A student claims: "Only Westerners are ethnocentric." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Ethnocentrism is a general human tendency found in all societies; anthropology tries to counter it everywhere, including in the anthropologist's own assumptions.
items.markingKey: Ethnocentrism is a general human tendency found in all societies; anthropology tries to counter it everywhere, including in the anthropologist's own assumptions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between culture and society.
items.answer: Society refers to the organised relationships and institutions connecting a group of people; culture refers to the learned, shared and contested meanings, values and practices through which they make sense of life.
items.markingKey: Society refers to the organised relationships and institutions connecting a group of people; culture refers to the learned, shared and contested meanings, values and practices through which they make sense of life. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between social and cultural anthropology and sociology.
items.answer: Both study social life, but anthropology traditionally relies on long-term participant observation and holistic, comparative study of small-scale or local settings, whereas sociology more often uses surveys and statistics to study large-scale patterns in industrial societies; the boundary is now blurred.
items.markingKey: Both study social life, but anthropology traditionally relies on long-term participant observation and holistic, comparative study of small-scale or local settings, whereas sociology more often uses surveys and statistics to study large-scale patterns in industrial societies; the boundary is now blurred. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between moral relativism and cultural relativism.
items.answer: Cultural relativism is a method: understand a practice in its own context before evaluating it. Moral relativism is a philosophical claim that no cross-cultural moral judgement is possible; most anthropologists accept the first but not necessarily the second.
items.markingKey: Cultural relativism is a method: understand a practice in its own context before evaluating it. Moral relativism is a philosophical claim that no cross-cultural moral judgement is possible; most anthropologists accept the first but not necessarily the second. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918)) as your example, describe how materiality is shown.
items.answer: Kula valuables are rarely worn or used; their value lies in their histories and the names of past holders, so objects carry social biographies and prestige rather than utility.

items.stem: Briefly describe Malinowski's fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands (1915–1918) and explain what it reveals about holism.
items.answer: Malinowski lived among Trobrianders for long periods, learned the language and traced how the kula exchange was linked to magic, canoe-building, chiefship and myth. He showed that the kula could only be understood by connecting exchange to politics, religion, technology and kinship rather than treating it as trade alone.

Describe, with examples from the text, how the traders in the text depend on and use clothing. Focus on what the people in the text do and say, not on your interpretation of it.
items.answer: Bales are opened unseen and their contents determine income ("feeds my children" or "rags"); clothing has names that carry meaning ("obroni wawu"); stalls are inherited (Ama's mother's stall); traders wore their best garments during the protest march.
items.markingKey: Bales are opened unseen and their contents determine income ("feeds my children" or "rags"); clothing has names that carry meaning ("obroni wawu"); stalls are inherited (Ama's mother's stall); traders wore their best garments during the protest march. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

At the bus depot on the edge of the city, Wairimu sells boiled eggs and peeled oranges from a tray balanced on a crate. "I am not a hawker," she tells me firmly. "Hawkers run. I have my place." Her place is a square of pavement she rents informally from the man who sweeps the depot each morning. When conductors shout the names of destinations, she calls back their nicknames. On Sundays she brings eggs to the sweeper's family instead of money. Twice a month the county askaris clear the pavement, and on those days Wairimu sits on the bus with her tray, "travelling" until they leave.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a bus depot in a Kenyan town.

Analyse why Wairimu insists that she is "not a hawker". Support your answer with evidence from the text. Support each step of your explanation with evidence from the extract.
items.answer: Her claim is an emic category that asserts status and identity: having "a place" signals legitimacy, belonging and respectability compared with mobile hawkers. Her security rests on social relations (sweeper, conductors) rather than legal title, so identity and place are produced through relationships and contested by state power (askaris).

items.stem: Using Abu-Lughod's critique of the "saving Muslim women" discourse after 2001 as an example, explain othering and the limits of ethnocentric judgement.
items.answer: She showed how images of veiled Afghan women were used to justify the war in Afghanistan, while ignoring women's own priorities and the harms of intervention. It shows that portraying women as passive victims of "their culture" erases their agency and serves political ends; she argues for respecting different ideas of a good life while still opposing injustice.

Link: it shows that portraying women as passive victims of "their culture" erases their agency and serves political ends; she argues for respecting different ideas of a good life while still opposing injustice. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to othering and the limits of ethnocentric judgement.

items.stem: Using Basso's work with the Western Apache of Cibecue as an example, explain space-place-time.
items.answer: Apache speakers used place-names and their stories to remind wrongdoers of ancestral lessons. It shows that space becomes place through names, stories and memory, and that places carry moral and historical meaning.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Social and cultural anthropology can never be truly comparative, because every culture is unique."
items.answer: Comparison is possible and valuable if concepts are used carefully and local meanings are respected.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Boas's historical particularism stresses that each culture has its own history; concepts such as "marriage" may not translate between societies (Gough on the Nayar). Arguments against: comparison need not deny uniqueness; it uses shared concepts to highlight difference; comparative work, such as on exchange (Malinowski, Weiner), has produced powerful insights; IB key concepts provide a framework for comparing across contexts. Supported judgement: Comparison is possible and valuable if concepts are used carefully and local meanings are respected.

items.stem: "Ethnocentrism can never be fully overcome by an anthropologist." Discuss.
items.answer: It cannot be eliminated completely, but it can be recognised and greatly reduced through reflexive practice.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: researchers always interpret through their own background (positionality); language and categories carry assumptions. Arguments against: reflexivity, long-term fieldwork and learning the language reduce ethnocentrism; collaboration with participants and critique by colleagues expose bias. Supported judgement: It cannot be eliminated completely, but it can be recognised and greatly reduced through reflexive practice. Markbands (10 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the Saturday clothing market of Kotei, sellers unpack bales of second-hand garments shipped from Europe. Buyers call the clothes "dead white men's clothes", though the sellers prefer "obroni wawu". Ama, who has sold there for twenty years, opens each bale like a lottery. "One bale feeds my children for a month, another one is rags." Her stall is her late mother's, and older traders still greet her by her mother's name. When a city council project proposed moving the market to a new concrete building, the traders marched with their best garments draped across their shoulders.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a second-hand clothing market in Ghana.

With reference to materiality, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Holmes's Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies. Keep the comparison running throughout rather than treating each case separately.
items.answer: Text: The bales link traders to global flows of discarded Western goods, over which they have no control; the names given to the clothes comment on that inequality; the council's relocation plan shows state power over space; the traders turn the clothes into a symbol in protest, showing materiality as a resource for resisting power. Ethnography – Seth M. Holmes, Fresh Fruit, Broken Bodies: Migrant Farmworkers in the United States (2013), with Triqui Indigenous migrants from Oaxaca, Mexico, on berry farms in Washington State and in California (fieldwork 2003–2005): Picking berries while bent over for hours damages backs and knees, so the body records structural inequality as chronic pain and injury. Comparison: similarities and differences in how materiality is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Compare and contrast how culture is shown in Horace Miner, "Body Ritual among the Nacirema" (1956) and Margaret Mead, Coming of Age in Samoa (1928).
items.answer: Miner's "Body Ritual among the Nacirema" (in a satirical article in American Anthropologist describing everyday American hygiene as exotic ritual): By describing Americans ("Nacirema" is American spelled backwards) brushing teeth and visiting doctors as magical rites, Miner showed how ethnographic language can make the familiar strange. Mead's Coming of Age in Samoa (among adolescent girls on Ta'ū in the Manu'a Islands of American Samoa (fieldwork 1925–1926)): Mead argued that adolescence in Samoa was relatively free of the stress seen in the United States, supporting Boas's view that culture rather than biology shapes development; Derek Freeman's 1983 critique disputed her findings. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far culture is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.
